Same logic for the 3D scene. Start with an image, the workflow recreates it as a 2D retro game scene. Then, it extracts all the assets needed (first in 2D then in 3D).

I imported all the scene assets in Unreal Engine to create a little street

I used Unreal’s Third Person Template to turn my character into a playable third person pov character.

caption_text:
Untitled Spaces - Blender Short Film

This project is the result of my passion for architecture, interior design, cinematography and music. Everything you see is 100% CGI (no AI of course), created using the free 3D software @blender.official The score is also composed by me, and best enjoyed through some proper speakers or headphones. Hope you like it :)

I went deep into the compositing stage for this project, drawing lots of inspiration from mid century architectural magazines. When scanned in they usually show a combination of film characteristics, half toning and CMYK print misalignment from the printing stage as well as imperfections and artificial sharpening from the digital processing and scanning of the catalogues. I wondered what would happen if I tried transferring these looks onto video, which is what I've tried doing in this project. I think the imperfections and abnormalities in stuff is what gives it character and what makes it relatable and realistic. It's a shame that the Youtube compression is so tough though, so I'd recommend watching it in full 4K. 

The programs I used in the project was Blender for all of the set layout, modeling, lighting texturing and rendering. The compositing was done in After Effects and the final sequence was edited in Davinci Resolve. For the scoring, it was composed in Logic Pro X. 

All of these shots are inspired by real world architects and furniture designers such as: 

Rem Koolhaas, Charles & Ray Eames, John Lautner, Hans & Florence Knoll, Kazuo Shinohara, Bahk Jong Sun, Wilhelm Wagenfeld, Paul Rudolph, André Lurcat, Verner Panton and David Bowen.

caption_text:
Temporal Strata | audiovisual dome experience
World premiere in Miami

Temporal Strata takes the materiality of time as its point of departure, treating time as strata capable of sedimentation, disturbance, and continuous formation. Within the immersive field of the dome, sound and image are woven into a single perceptual space, displacing linear narrative as the mode through which time is apprehended. Time is instead progressively recalibrated in the act of looking and listening, as rhythms elongate and restructure and attention shifts between micro-variations. The work invites consciousness to contract into a single point, converting time from abstract measure into a state perceived through sound and image. Amid the accumulation of texture and the collapse of space, one begins to gauge the sense of presence that each breath inscribes.

caption_text:
Cymbal interaction test - animation & audio //

This is an early test of modeling, animating and rendering believable cymbal behavior, for a bigger project of a complete drum kit animated and rendered in Cinema 4D

The drumstick is traditionally (and somewhat sloppy) animated using keyframes, the cymbal utilizes Signal by @greyscalegorilla for the tilting and the micro vibrations. There are two Signal tags, constantly running in a loop, one on the rotation axis of a null, and another on the strength parameter of a bend deformer (actually it's two bend deformers, but one is just following the other, but flipped) and I'm just manually keyframing the volume of the Signal tags to correspond with the hits.

The audio is made using Superior Drummer 3 by @toontrack which I'll also be using when I finally get to animate the full kit!

creator: guido.glid
description: 待分析：CG 判定、物件、動態、材質與顏色尚未完成核對。
caption_text:
Our @swatch Colors of Joy film just received Video of the Year at @motiondesignawards ♥️
 
We are really happy about this one, mostly because when we made this video, we decided not to show the project in the usual way. Even though Colors of Joy was part of a full 360 campaign, we wanted to show it through the eyes of the creatives behind it. So this film became a sort of collage of process.... raw ideas, unfinished renders, previews, tests, playful moments, things half-built, things still searching for their final form.

Probably 80% of what you see in that video is not “finished” in the traditional sense. And that was exactly the point. We wanted to show the energy behind the work. The exploration. The experimentation. The fun. The human thinking behind the final campaign.

This award shows that the community still cares deeply about the PROCESS and HOW things are made. Not just what the final image looks like, but what is behind it..... the attempts, the doubts, the play, the decisions, the people who made it, what was tried, what failed, what evolved.

At a moment when final images are becoming easier and easier to generate, this feels like an important reminder to everyone: the value is not only in the final pixel. It is in the vision, the craft, the taste, the time, the story, the experimentation, and the human energy behind it.

That is what gives a project its soul.

It means a lot to see that raw ideas, unfinished moments, and honest creative process can still resonate.

And maybe that is exactly why our videos cut through the noise.

A huge thank you to everyone involved in this project, to Motion Design Awards for the recognition, and to the creative community for embracing unconventional work like this.

Material [Fundamentals]

Full circle: Photographing a 3D render.

In the next phase of our crossover experiment with @mariuswhansen, we flipped the traditional workflow on its head.

After finishing our 3D compositing, we returned to Marius’s studio with our final renders displayed on high-resolution screens. By re-photographing those displays using physical lenses, anamorphic correction, and multi-exposure techniques, we captured beautifully unexpected in-camera results.

The resulting images have the ethereal presence of genuine physical objects, grounded by practical studio lighting, and blur the line between tangible reality and digital artefact.​

caption_text:
🇬🇧 🖥️ The art of Federico Piccirillo: 3D artist & motion designer

There are artists who use 3D to recreate reality. Federico Piccirillo uses it to reinvent it. In this post, we take a brief look at the Italian motion designer and art director whose work creates images suspended somewhere between the possible and the imaginary, oscillating between surrealism and hyperrealism. Each animation becomes the construction of a digital space where light and materials, in just a few seconds, are able to tell a story. Simple forms, minimalist environments, and warm color palettes become tools for creating images that feel both familiar and impossible, often elevated by a perfectly chosen soundtrack. The reason I decided to feature Federico on this page is his close albeit indirect connection to the world of cinema, recalling a cinematic language that does not merely imitate reality, but transforms it into emotion. This approach is evident throughout his work, where every frame feels as though it were conceived as a shot from a film.

After earning a degree in Graphic Design and Visual Communication in Florence, Piccirillo began his professional career as a motion designer at Nerdo Studio. He later chose to work as a freelance artist, specializing in 3D and collaborating on campaigns for brands such as Google, Nike, Apple, LEGO, IBM, Oppo, and many others. What makes his work truly distinctive, however, is not a single recognizable style. On the contrary, Piccirillo deliberately avoids confining himself to one visual language, constantly experimenting with new aesthetics and new ways of telling stories through movement. This ongoing exploration demonstrates that 3D is not merely a technical tool, but a powerful expressive medium capable of transforming ideas, emotions, and imagination into living images.

title: Fluid study · 2D Pyro
creator: droikcg
description: 待分析：CG 判定、物件、動態、材質與顏色尚未完成核對。 本項暫為輪播封面，完整媒體拆分待後續分析。
caption_text:
This fluid study was built around a custom 2D Pyro workflow.

The idea originally came from an R&D task I was working on for a client project earlier this year. I liked the underlying behavior enough to revisit it later and push the technique further as a personal experiment.

I first created an initial simulation focused on the main velocity field, while also generating UVs internally as an additional 2D Pyro field. That first sim then became the advection driver for the bubbles and their velocity, allowing them to inherit the motion and flow of the fluid in a more natural way.

After that, I created a second fluid simulation using only the velocity from the first Pyro setup, combined with collisions and bubble velocity. This made the fluid react to spheres moving across its surface, changing the internal mixing and creating more dynamic interaction.

I also experimented with a non-divergent workflow in COPs, but for this particular look it was missing some of the organic, naturally unstable motion that I still get from the old 2D Pyro Solver.

A fun experiment in using Pyro not only as smoke, but as a flexible field-based solver for art-directable fluid motion and procedural detail.

title: The Ascension and Exodus of PAK
creator: davidariew
description: 待分析：CG 判定、物件、動態、材質與顏色尚未完成核對。 本項暫為輪播封面，完整媒體拆分待後續分析。
caption_text:
“The Ascension of PAK” and “The Exodus of PAK” are two sides of the same visual and sonic idea.

For the sound design, I wanted the relationship between the two pieces to feel almost like looking at the same image through a negative: familiar shapes, movements, and gestures, but emotionally inverted.
Rather than creating two completely separate soundtracks, I approached them as sonic mirror images. The same core sonic language exists in both pieces, but its emotional weight, frequency, texture, dynamics, and spatial character are transformed between the positive and negative versions.

"Ascension" lives in the world of emergence, elevation, expansion, and light. Its sounds are designed to feel as though they are pulling upward and opening outward. Longer tonal elements, rising textures, resonances, and brighter high-frequency detail help reinforce the sense of movement and transformation.

"Exodus" takes that same conceptual DNA and turns it inside out. Sounds become darker, heavier, more restrained, and more gravitational. Where Ascension suggests expansion, Exodus suggests contraction. Where one rises, the other falls.

A major part of the process was building the sound effects around the physical movement of the visuals. Every transition, distortion, flicker, rotation, flash, and change in form became an opportunity for a sonic event. Impacts were synchronized to visual hits, granular textures followed digital artifacts, tonal sweeps reinforced movement through space, and subtle environmental layers helped give the abstract imagery a sense of physical presence.

I wanted the sound design to respond to the black-and-white inversion itself. The visual negative isn't simply a different grade—it changes how the image feels. I treated the audio in the same way.

The two tracks share DNA, but their emotional frequencies are reversed.

The goal was for the two pieces to feel like they could exist independently, while revealing something completely different when experienced together—as two reflections of the same sonic and visual object.

caption_text:
We’ve wanted this camera for years.

A small, anamorphic, fixed-lens digital camera built specifically around a dedicated 65:24 frame.

No one made it.

So we did.

This is the GX-P1.

It’s not a render. It’s a real working camera on my desk right now. We’ve shot nearly 3,000 images with it already, taken it to three different countries, and put together a small team of friends; @ashthorp (yeah the freakin guy who designed the Bat-Mobile!) and Matt Bernath, for design and software respectively. @gxace developed countless prototypes and learned CNC machining to bring this camera to life.

We’re working through the software, electronics, optics, controls and finding manufacturing partners now, with the goal of crowdfunding GX-P1 by the end of the year. 

There is a lot more we haven’t shown yet, and it’s physically hard to stop ourselves from telling more.

It’s an incredibly ambitious project for us but we are building something from our hearts, and we know that the dream of a camera like this isn’t just in our hearts alone. 

This is just the beginning.

Go to GxAce.com/gxp1 to stay in the loop and hear news first.

title: Token framework · UI system
creator: atom63_
description: 待分析：CG 判定、物件、動態、材質與顏色尚未完成核對。
caption_text:
Lately, I’ve been building a foundational system designed to support everything I want to ship through rapid prototyping and AI-assisted development. While "vibe coding" lets us spin up ideas in minutes, it also exposes a major gap: without strong structural boundaries, rapid code quickly turns into a black box of technical debt.

The goal isn't just to build fast; it's to define efficient, transparent patterns that keep the architecture predictable.

Some progress on the token framework. It currently supports:
→ Multi-axis theming contracts for dynamic UI skins.
→ System modes configured for macOS and Windows structural paradigms.
→ A wallpaper package that extracts and feeds dynamic primary colors back into the UI.
→ Granular exposed controls for fluid typography, corner radiuses, and system iconography.
→ A unified theme package that instantly drops into independent micro-sites consuming the same tokens.

It’s easier than ever to code something visually stunning. But because UI is deeply subjective and constantly evolving, the real engineering challenge changes:

How do you build an infrastructure that isn't just adaptive to any art direction—but remains maintainable, deterministic, and meaningful?

Still exploring the edges of this, but unwrapping that black box is the part worth solving.

Live site: https://os.atom63.io/
Deeply inspired by @ryo.lu
